stages.name: Observe
stages.instruction: Each dot is a $^{235}\text{U}$ nucleus in a fuel pellet. A stray neutron hits one, splitting it into two lighter daughters plus $\nu$ fresh neutrons — those seed new fissions in a chain reaction. Sweep the multiplication factor $k$ (moving the absorber rod), toggle LOG, and let the sim run past one effective half-life.
stages.concept: For $N_0$ fissile nuclei consumed in a chain, $N(t) = N_0\,e^{-k\,t\,/\,\tau_0}$ with $\tau_0$ a fixed characteristic time of the pellet geometry. Higher $k$ = more neutrons per fission survive to trigger the next one = fuel burns faster. Because the daughters are more tightly bound than the parent ($E_l/A$ hook), every fission releases $Q > 0$.

stages.name: Experiment
stages.instruction: A mystery core's power-decay curve (bright orange) is drawn over the plot with three sample points. Adjust the absorber to tune $k$ until your simulated core matches within $\pm 5\%$.
stages.concept: Two cores with the same $k$ burn through their fuel at the same relative rate. On a log plot, matching slopes = matching $k$: the slope is $-k\,/\,\tau_0$.

stages.name: Evaluate
stages.instruction: Reactor logbook only. Three noisy assay readings $(t, N)$ from a shielded core are given — no live sim, no rod. Compute $k = \tau_0 \,\ln(N_1/N_2)\,/\,(t_2 - t_1)$ and enter it. Peek reveals the true decay curve for $1.5$ s (never the value of $k$).
stages.concept: From any two readings: $\lambda_{\mathrm{eff}} = \dfrac{\ln(N_1/N_2)}{t_2 - t_1}$, so $k = \tau_0 \, \lambda_{\mathrm{eff}}$. On a log-$N$ plot the slope is $-k\,/\,\tau_0$; $\tau_0 = 20$ u for this pellet.

labels.tip1: sweep k, toggle LOG, let the sim run
labels.tip2: match the bright orange target — try LOG for a linear fit
labels.tip3: compute λ_eff from two points, then k = τ₀ · λ_eff

1.1: k is the multiplication factor — the average number of new neutrons each fission produces that go on to trigger another fission.
1.2: Toggle LOG: on a log scale, N(t) is a straight line whose slope equals −k/τ₀. Higher k → steeper slope.
1.3: The dashed teal curve is the analytic N₀·exp(−k·t/τ₀); the solid orange is the stochastic count. They agree on average — the variance is real Poisson noise.

2.1: The bright orange curve is the target reactor. Match the slope, not just the endpoints.
2.2: On LOG, curves with the same k are parallel straight lines. On linear, the target crosses N₀/2 at t = τ₀·ln 2 / k.
2.3: The Δ readout in the top-right shows how far your k is from the target. Under 5% wins.

3.1: Pick any two readings (t₁, N₁) and (t₂, N₂). Then λ_eff = ln(N₁/N₂) / (t₂ − t₁), and k = τ₀ · λ_eff with τ₀ = 20 u.
3.2: On the LOG plot the assay dots line up. The slope of that line is −k/τ₀ — read it off the axes if you prefer graphical to algebraic.
3.3: Tolerance is ±3%; the readings are noisy so small rounding differences are fine. Peek gives you the true curve for 1.5 s — it does NOT give you k.
